newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N., Iraq haggle over food observers' duties.
newsitem.headline: U.N., Iraq haggle over food observers' duties.

text.p: The United Nations is short of cash to hire food distribution observers and is still haggling with Iraq over issues that must be resolved before Iraqis can benefit from an oil-for-food deal, diplomats said on Monday.
They said the United Nations had completed the nomination of the 151 international staff needed to monitor the distribution of food but was short of money to recruit them.
"If they are not in place I do not believe there will be any distribution of food from the oil sales," said one diplomat.

Iraq began exporting crude oil last month under a deal with the United Nations allowing it to export $2 billion worth of oil in six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian supplies to help offset the effects of sanctions imposed since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
An escrow account holding the money from the sales was supposed to have received nearly $200 million by Monday, a U.N. spokesman in New York said on Friday.

He said $53.1 million had been disbursed from the account so far, including $33.9 million for the Geneva-based U.N. compensation commission that rules on reparations for victims of the Iraqi invasion. The remainder went for various other U.N. activities related to the 1991 Gulf War that ended Iraq's occupation of Kuwait.

A Security Council sanctions committee has approved a number of food contracts submitted by Iraq but diplomats said no money had yet been paid by Iraq via the escrow account at the New York branch of the Banque Nationale de Paris.
"Even if contracts are made I do not see how food could be shipped into Iraq and stored if the observers are not in place," said one diplomat.
He said the United Nations also needed to clear up differences with the Iraqi side on the observers' duties and their freedom of movement before the start of any food distribution.
The observers will try to ensure that food and medical supplies from the oil sales are being handed out equitably.

"The U.N. needs to pay the observers, supply them with vehicles, pay for their lodging and accommodation and furnish them with necessary communications gear. Without money it cannot do so," the diplomat said.
Iraqis were furious on hearing that first allocations from their oil money did not go for food and medicine.

"The so-called victims of the war and U.N. arms inspectors could have waited a week or two. But there is little chance for the dying baby in the hospital to survive," said a teacher father of four whose monthly salary of 3,500 dinars is hardly enough to buy one chicken.
U.N. statistics show that 4,500 Iraqi children under five die because of sanctions and more than five million Iraqis do not have enough food to eat.
More money from the oil sales will flow into Iraq's escrow account but the delay is certain to worsen the hardships of ordinary Iraqis waiting anxiously for new rations from the deal.
The current government rations, the United Nations says, barely cover one-third of the people's needs.
